b.bio: Born Bernardino Bacchini on 31 August 1651 at Borgo San Donnino in the Duchy of Parma, he entered the Order of St. Benedict in 1668. He served as secretary to the abbot of St. Benedict of Ferrara, became theologian to the duke of Parma in 1688, was appointed counsellor of the Inquisition by the duke of Modena in 1691, later librarian to that duke, and prior of his order at Modena in 1704. He died at Ferrara on 1 September 1721. He is known for the editio princeps of Andreas Agnellus' Liber Pontificalis Ecclesiae Ravennatis.
b.s: The works held here are his prefatory, dedicatory, and critical apparatus defending Leo the Great's authorship and Chalcedonian reception of the Tome against Agnellus, Dupin, Vossius, and Dominicus Mita, alongside observations on Peter Chrysologus.

b.bio: Sources under this name describe two different twelfth-century writers: Baldric of Dol (c. 1050–1130), abbot of Bourgueil and bishop of Dol, author of a First Crusade history; and Balderic of Florennes, a scholar of Paris who headed the cathedral school at Trier and later served as provost of Saint Simeon in the Porta Nigra. The latter met Archbishop Albero of Trier at Paris in 1147, became his friend and adviser, and after Albero's death wrote his biography, the Gesta Alberonis. He disappears from the record after 1163.
b.s: The library holds only a brief historical notice under this name (PL 134); readers seeking his known work should consult the Gesta Alberonis, printed elsewhere in Migne (PL 154).

b.bio: Born at Meung-sur-Loire, most likely in 1046 (the Catholic Encyclopedia gives about 1050), Baldric studied at Angers and entered the Abbey of Bourgueil in Anjou, becoming prior around 1077 and abbot by 1089 (the Catholic Encyclopedia dates his abbacy from 1079). In 1107 he received the pallium from Paschal II as bishop of Dol-en-Bretagne, made archbishop in 1108 (Arlima dates his archiepiscopate from 1107), an office he held until his death on January 5/7, 1130 (Arlima gives January 5, at Préaux). He attended church councils, traveled to Rome and England, worked to reform monastic discipline, and spent his last years in retirement.
b.s: His Historia Hierosolymitana is a four-book account of the First Crusade drawn partly from eyewitness testimony and submitted for correction to Peter of Maillesais; the library also holds eight works under his name across PL 162 and PL 166, including his poems, hagiographies of Robert of Arbrissel, Hugh of Rouen, and Valentine, and his Itinerary to the Fécamp monks.

b.bio: The library prints the name as Balduinus Flandriae et Hannoniae: Baldwin, count of Flanders (as Baldwin IX) and of Hainaut (as Baldwin VI). He was one of the most prominent leaders of the Fourth Crusade, which took Constantinople in 1204, and was crowned the first Latin emperor. Defeated by Kaloyan of Bulgaria at Adrianople in 1205, he spent his last days as a prisoner. The eight pages held here are not theology but his letters and diplomas: truce terms with the sultan of Babylon, arbitration panels, commerce guarantees, and retaliation law, addressed to John of England, Robert earl of Leicester, and Emperor Isaac.
b.s: The works here are charters and letters showing how a crusader count governed — truces, oaths, mixed arbitration, and civic obligations — rather than doctrinal writing; readers should treat them as legal-diplomatic evidence, not patristic theology.

w: Privilege for the Church of Bethlehem

b.bio: Baldwin of Boulogne, youngest son of Count Eustace II of Boulogne and Ida of Lorraine, was first marked for a clerical career, then joined the First Crusade under his brother Godfrey of Bouillon. He seized Edessa in 1098 as its first Latin count and succeeded Godfrey as king of Jerusalem in 1100, reigning until his death at Al-Arish on 2 April 1118. The work held here is not a theological treatise but a royal privilege: a diploma elevating the church of Bethlehem to episcopal dignity, citing papal authority (Paschal II) and grounding the elevation in the crusade's divine accomplishment.
b.s: The library holds his privilege for the Church of Bethlehem, a charter asserting that kingship rests on divine nod and popular election and that Bethlehem deserves episcopal rank — evidence of how crusader kings exercised ecclesiastical authority.

b.bio: Baptista Mantuanus (Battista Spagnoli), born at Mantua 17 April 1447, died there 22 March 1516. Eldest son of Peter Spagnoli, a Spanish nobleman at the Mantuan court, he studied grammar under Gregorio Tifernate and philosophy at Pavia under Polo Bagelardi. After a period of disorder in his youth he entered the reformed Carmelite convent at Ferrara in 1463–64, was ordained at Bologna, taught philosophy and divinity there, tutored the children of the Duke of Mantua, and served as vicar general and later general of his congregation. He was beatified in 1890.
b.s: A leading Latin poet of the Renaissance whose hagiographic verse — represented here by an encomiastic poem on a saint's life treating providential dreams, temptation overcome, divine inspiration replacing human teachers in scripture, and the sanctity of the saint's death day as entry into heaven — made him widely read in schools and devotional contexts.

b.bio: The library holds one work under this name, a Letter to Suger printed in PL 181. the surviving records describe three different medieval Bartholomews — the Dominican canonist Bartholomew of San Concordio (c. 1260–1347), the Dominican hagiographer Bartholomew of Trent (c. 1200–1251), and the Franciscan encyclopedist Bartholomaeus Anglicus (before 1203–1272) — none of whom is identified as 'Bartholomew of Châlons' or connected to a letter to Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis. No source gives dates, offices, or biographical facts for this author, so none are asserted here.
b.s: His place in this library rests on a single item, a letter addressed to Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis preserved in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 181.

b.bio: Bartholomew of Laon is identified with Barthélemy de Jur (also called de Grandson or de Joux), son of Conon Falcon, seigneur de Grandson. Raised in the household of his maternal great-uncle Manassès II, archbishop of Reims, he served as treasurer of the cathedral chapters of Laon (from 1102) and Saint-Quentin (from 1106) before being elected bishop of Laon in 1113, consecrated at Rheims in the presence of Louis VI. He contributed his own money to rebuilding Laon Cathedral after the commune's revolt of 1112.
b.s: The single work held here is a donation charter granting the site of Prémontré to Norbert in perpetuity, freeing church lands from exaction and exempting religious houses from parochial tithes, with an anathema on violators — an early witness to the foundation of the Premonstratensian order.

b.bio: A Bartholomew of the monastery of Marmoutier ('Majoris monasterii'), known only through a single letter preserved in PL 149 addressed to an Ernald. No dates, offices, or further biography are supported by any available evidence; The surviving records describe other men of the same name (Bartholomew of San Concordio and Bartholomaeus Anglicus) and cannot be used for this author.
b.s: His letter to Ernald is a polemical and historical objection against the bishop of Le Mans, defending an episcopal donation of an altar made in perpetuity and arguing that chapter confirmations bind successors inviolably and that confirmed matters are exempt from new judgment.

b.bio: Benedictus Crispus, archbishop of Milan from about 685 until his death in March 732 (though one source gives 725), was a Lombard-era prelate and poet. He wrote the epitaph for Caedwalla, king of Wessex, buried in St. Peter's in Rome, and composed a verse medical manual drawing on Pliny and Quintus Serenus. In Rome under Pope Constantine he contested the claim of Armentarius of Pavia that Pavia was immediately subject to the Roman see, arguing that Pavia historically belonged to the metropolitan see of Milan; the pope ruled against him.
b.s: The works held here are his Epitaphium Ceadual, a Poematium medicum of herbal remedies, and the Querimonia in synodo — verse documents of Lombard-era Milanese ecclesiastical politics and medical learning.

b.bio: Benedictus I, son of Boniface, was bishop of Rome from his consecration on 2 June 575 until his death on 30 July 579. His election followed John III by nearly eleven months because imperial confirmation from Constantinople was delayed by the Lombard advance. His pontificate coincided with the Lombard invasion, famine, plague, and flooding of the Tiber; a grain fleet sent by Emperor Justin II relieved Rome. He consecrated twenty-one bishops and raised Gregory I to the diaconate. The Greeks called him Bonosus. The single page held here is his epistle against the Arians and the Baetican deniers.
b.s: His surviving epistle shows a Roman bishop enforcing orthodoxy against Arians in Visigothic Spain, defending the Trinity, baptismal formula, and the church as pillar of truth.

b.bio: Benedict II was a Roman, son of John, trained in the schola cantorum and noted for his knowledge of Scripture. Elected in 683 but ordained only on 26 June 684 after awaiting imperial permission from Constantine IV (Pogonatus), he served as bishop of Rome until his death on 8 May 685. He obtained from the emperor a decree easing or abolishing imperial confirmation of papal elections, worked to secure Spanish episcopal subscriptions to the Sixth General Council against Monothelitism, sought the submission of Macarius, ex-Bishop of Antioch, and supported Wilfrid of York. The letter held here is the one printed at PL 96:423 to the Spanish bishops.
b.s: The work held here is his letter urging the Spanish bishops (under King Ervigius) to subscribe to the Sixth Council's definition, arguing that subscription to conciliar definition proves catholic faith and that right confession attains the heavenly kingdom.

b.bio: Benedict III was a Roman, son of Peter, made cardinal-priest of San Callisto by Leo IV and elected pope on Leo's death in July 855. His election was contested: the legates sent to the emperors were won over to the excommunicated cardinal Anastasius, who was briefly installed while Benedict was imprisoned; popular resistance restored Benedict, who was consecrated on 29 September or 6 October 855 and later admitted Anastasius to lay communion. He wrote to the Frankish bishops reproaching their silence amid the disorders oppressing the church in the empire.
b.s: The letters here assert papal primacy in discipline: synodal decrees ratified by the apostolic see stand permanently, metropolitans answer only to the Roman pontiff, clerics may be summoned to Rome for judgment, and excommunication excludes from the Lord's body and blood while aiming at the sinner's salvation.

b.bio: A Roman, son of Mammalus, ordained priest by Pope Formosus and pope from early 900 until his death in the summer of 903. Flodoard called him 'the Great' for his noble birth and generosity. His recorded acts include crowning Louis the Blind emperor in 901, excommunicating Baldwin II of Flanders for the murder of Archbishop Fulk of Reims, upholding Formosus's decision in favor of Argrim's claim to Langres, supporting Stephen of Naples, and aiding Malacenus of Amasia, driven from his see by the Saracens.
b.s: The two short works held here — letters and a privilege — show a tenth-century pope asserting that a canonically elected bishop holds his see lawfully and that papal privilege may revise a predecessor's judgment, as in his support for Argrim against Teutbald at Langres.

b.bio: Benedict IX, born Theophylact of the Tusculani family in Rome, was pope three times: 1032–1044, April–May 1045, and 1047–1048. Placed on the see as a youth by his father Count Alberic of Tusculum, nephew of Benedict VIII and John XIX, he was driven out by a Roman revolt, resigned in favor of his godfather Gregory VI, returned, and was finally deposed alongside Sylvester III and Gregory VI at the Council of Sutri summoned under Henry III. He died at Grottaferrata around 1055/56. The library holds only his letters and diplomas from PL 141 — chiefly privileges for churches and monasteries.
b.s: The works here are not treatises but papal diplomas granting monasteries exemption from episcopal and secular jurisdiction, free abbatial election, and powers of absolution and ordination under threat of anathema — documents central to the eleventh-century contest over church property and jurisdiction.

w: Life X of St. Thomas of Canterbury

b.bio: Benedict of Peterborough, place and date of birth unknown, died 29 September 1193. He was educated at Oxford, served as chancellor to Archbishop Richard of Canterbury from 1174 and as prior of Christ Church, Canterbury from 1175, then received the abbacy of Peterborough from Henry II in 1177, holding it until his death. He belonged to the circle of Becket's admirers and wrote an account of Becket's Passion, preserved in part in the Quadrilogus, and a first-hand account of Becket's Miracles. He was formerly credited with the Gesta Henrici Regis Secundi, now attributed to Roger of Howden.
b.s: The library holds his Life of St. Thomas of Canterbury, a partisan history defending the liberty of the church against Henry II's justices and Becket's killers, arguing that no oath may be extorted from bishop or clerks, that bishops may absolve clerks unlawfully bound by coerced oaths, that judgment of bishops belongs to the pope, and that a churchman must defend the liberty of the church unto death.

w: On Imperial Power in the City of Rome

b.t: Latin chronicler; a monk (order not specified in the sources)
b.bio: A monk at the monastery of St. Andrew on Mount Soracte near Rome, active in the tenth century. The Catholic Encyclopedia dates his chronicle to 968 and warns that it is filled with legends; the Austrian Academy database places him between roughly 950 and 1025, at Rome, and calls him simply a monk and chronicler. He should not be confused with Benedict, the twelfth-century canon of St. Peter's who wrote the Liber polypticus, nor with Benedict of Bari.
b.s: His chronicle is a tenth-century Roman history covering the church above all, the Lombard wars, and the city's deliverance from Greek rule — legendary in detail, but a witness to how a Roman monk narrated Narses, Totila, and Ambrose.

b.bio: Benedictus VI was a Roman, son of Hildebrand, and cardinal deacon of San Teodoro before his election as pope after the death of John XIII in September 972. Consecration waited until 19 January 973 for Emperor Otto I's approval. The sources record little of his pontificate beyond confirming privileges of churches and monasteries. In 974 a Roman aristocratic faction led by Crescentius and the deacon Boniface VII imprisoned him in Castel Sant'Angelo; he was strangled there to prevent his release by an imperial envoy. The work held here is letters and privileges from PL 135: grants asserting papal jurisdiction over metropolitans and the pallium, defense of monastic liberties against bishops, counts, and kings, condemnation of simony, and claims of Petrine authority — including that Peter personally founded the church of Trier.
b.s: His surviving letters are brief instruments of tenth-century papal government, showing how the see exercised delegated metropolitan jurisdiction and defended monastic exemption.

b.bio: Benedictus VII was bishop of Rome from October 974 until his death on 10 July 983. A Roman, son of David or Deodatus and nephew of Alberic II of Spoleto, he had been bishop of Sutri before being elected under the influence of Sicco, envoy of Emperor Otto II, as successor to the murdered Benedict VI and in place of the usurper Boniface VII. His pontificate, secured by Otto II's support, promoted monasticism and acted against simony, notably in an encyclical of 981 forbidding payment for conferring holy orders.
b.s: The works here are his letters and privileges—defenses of monastic exemption from all jurisdiction save the apostolic see, metropolitan dignity grounded in the antiquity of privilege, and the binding force of apostolic sanctions—directed against Salzburg, Abbot Leo, the simoniacs, and others; documents of tenth-century papal jurisdictional authority.

b.bio:
Benedictus VII (d. 10 July 983) — Benedictus VII was bishop of Rome from October 974 until his death on 10 July 983. A Roman, son of David or Deodatus and nephew of Alberic II of Spoleto, he had been bishop of Sutri before being elected under the influence of Sicco, envoy of Emperor Otto II, as successor to the murdered Benedict VI and in place of the usurper Boniface VII. His pontificate, secured by Otto II's support, promoted monasticism and acted against simony, notably in an encyclical of 981 forbidding payment for conferring holy orders.

Henricus II imperator (973–1024) — Henry II, called Saint Henry, was the last emperor of the Saxon (Ottonian) dynasty. Born 6 May 973 in Bavaria, he succeeded his father as Duke of Bavaria in 995, became King of the Romans after Otto III's death in 1002, King of Italy in 1004, and was crowned emperor by Pope Benedict VIII in 1014. Educated at the cathedral school of Hildesheim, he died without an heir on 13 July 1024 and was canonized by Pope Eugenius III in 1146. The library holds his charters and diplomas from PL 140: grants to churches and monasteries asserting perpetual donation, exemption from secular jurisdiction, and royal protection against burdensome advocates.
b.s: The works here are his letters and privileges—defenses of monastic exemption from all jurisdiction save the apostolic see, metropolitan dignity grounded in the antiquity of privilege, and the binding force of apostolic sanctions—directed against Salzburg, Abbot Leo, the simoniacs, and others; documents of tenth-century papal jurisdictional authority.

b.bio: Benedict VIII was born Theophylact of Tusculum, son of Count Gregory I of Tusculum, and became pope on 18 May 1012, imposed by force though a layman. He crowned Henry II emperor on 14 February 1014 and kept close ties with him; he suppressed the Crescentii, opposed Saracen attacks in southern Italy, held a synod at Pavia in 1022 against clerical incontinence and simony with the emperor, and supported the Cluniac reform and the Truce of God. His brother succeeded him as John XIX.
b.s: The letters and decrees held here are papal bulls defending monastic privilege: they assert that papal confirmation protects monastic privileges, that apostolic protection exempts monasteries from episcopal interdict, that a bishop may not interdict the monastic divine office, that monastic discipline belongs to the abbot rather than diocesan bishops, and that violation of papal privilege incurs anathema — directed against bishops such as John of Orvieto and Bruno of Langres and against secular rulers and simoniacal appointers.

b.bio: Berengar of Narbonne is listed in the Epistolae collection as an archbishop of Narbonne to whom Pope Adrian IV addressed letters. He should not be confused with Berengar of Tours (d. 1088), the eleventh-century theologian of the eucharistic controversy. However, the complaint held here is directed against the archbishop of Narbonne himself, against Raimbald, archbishop of Arles, and against bishops of the diocese, over questions of jurisdiction, simony, excommunication, and lawful judgment.
b.s: The single work held here is a short polemical complaint arguing that selling holy orders is simony condemned by the church, that excommunication by an unjust excommunicate bishop is void, that ecclesiastical disputes require lawful judgment before penalty, and that absolution belongs to the apostolic see.

w: Exposition on the Seven Visions of the Book of Revelation

b.bio: Berengaudus is the name attached to the Expositio super septem visiones libri Apocalypsis, a Latin commentary on Revelation. Tradition makes him a Benedictine monk of Ferrières Abbey in the time of Lupus Servatus (840–892), but the attribution has been questioned: some scholars date the work closer to the twelfth century, others place its author around 1040 or as a contemporary of Anselm of Laon. Derk Visser defends the traditional ninth-century identification from the commentary's familiarity with Haimo of Auxerre and an internal acrostic. The work circulated widely in manuscript by the twelfth century; it was once printed under Ambrose's name following Cuthbert Tunstall. A work 'De incarnacione uerbi' is also attributed to him in medieval catalogues.
b.s: His Apocalypse commentary was widely copied in medieval England (attested in numerous monastic booklists) and was used in the Douce Apocalypse (c. 1270), where French translations of its text accompany the Latin.

w: On the Miracles of St. Faith

b.bio: Bernard of Angers was a student of Fulbert of Chartres and later master of the cathedral school of Angers. He made three pilgrimages to the shrine of Saint Faith at Conques in Rouergue during the 1010s and 1020s, arriving as a skeptic who suspected the saint's miracles were inventions, and left as her recorder: he wrote the first two books of the Liber miraculorum sancte Fidis, opening with a letter to Fulbert. The last two books were completed by anonymous authors after his death.
b.s: His Liber miraculorum sancte Fidis defends the truth of Saint Faith's miracles against those who deemed them fabricated — arguing that faith in them should rest on experience and that the truth of miracles outweighs elegance of style — while also serving as propaganda for the Conques sanctuary.

b.bio: Bernard II of Besalú, son of William I, was co-ruler with his brother William II from 1052 and sole count after William's assassination in 1066, a murder in which Bernard himself was suspected. He was a proponent of the Gregorian reforms and almost certainly joined the First Crusade. The library holds two short pieces under his name from PL 149: a letter to Bernard of Marseille and a diploma, both concerned with monastic reform.
b.s: These are letters of a lay magnate intervening in monastic reform: they argue that simoniacal abbots may be expelled without restitution, that the right to choose an abbot belongs to the reforming abbey, and that placing monasteries under reformed houses guards against heresy.

b.bio: A Frankish monk of the ninth century, known in some authorities as Bernard the Wise (Bernardus Sapiens). The sources give no birthplace or monastery and no dates beyond a floruit around 870. He wrote an account of a journey from Francia through Italy to Egypt and the Holy Land, describing Jerusalem's churches, Mount Sion, and sites in Egypt associated with Mark and the Holy Family.
b.s: The Itinerary held here is an early surviving Latin pilgrim account of the ninth-century Holy Land under Muslim rule, recording local traditions about apostolic sites, the Holy Fire at the Sepulchre, and conditions for Christians among the Saracens.

b.bio: Bernardus Guidonis (Bernard Gui) was born at Royères in the Limousin around 1261/62 and was received into the Dominican order by Stephen of Salanhac on 16 September 1280. He served as prior of several convents in southern France, acted as his order's representative in Rome, and from 1306 to 1324 was inquisitorial judge at Toulouse, experience reflected in his handbook for inquisitors. He became bishop of Tuy in 1323 and bishop of Lodève in 1324, dying on 30 December 1331 at Lauroux.
b.s: The library holds only a short biographical-historical piece (PL 179) treating the Church, Scripture, and the Trinity, asserting among other things that a council condemned Peter Abelard's teaching and that saints' miracles confirm the faith; readers should note this does not match the inquisitor's known Practica officii inquisitionis, so the attribution to the famous Bernard Gui should be treated cautiously.

w: Donation for the Church of St. Gregory of Rodez

b.bio: The library records an author printed as 'Bernard of Lodève', to whom it attributes a single one-page work, a Donation for the Church of St. Gregory of Rodez, preserved in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 150). No biographical details are supported for this author: surviving records concern Bernard Gui (Bernardus Guidonis), Bishop of Lodève, whose name-forms do not include 'Bernard of Lodève' in the authority variants, so they cannot safely be applied to this author.
b.s: The item held here is a minor administrative act (a donation charter) rather than a theological treatise; its author cannot be confidently identified with any figure described in The surviving records.

b.bio: Bernard of Toledo (also called Bernard of Sédirac or Bernard of Le Sauvetat) was born in Gascony around 1050, at La Sauvetat de Blanquefort near Agen, and died in Spain in 1125. A monk of Cluny, he was sent to Spain to further the reforms of Gregory VII, became abbot of St. Facundus at Sahagún in 1080, and was named archbishop of Toledo by Alfonso VI in 1086. Urban II raised his see to primatial dignity in 1088. He is often confused with Bernard of Agen, first bishop of Sigüenza.
b.s: Under his episcopate the church of Castile and León emerged from isolation and dependence on Rome; his works here are sermons preserved in PL 155.

w: Quick and True Division of the Monochord in the Diatonic Scale

b.bio: Bernelinus (Bernelin), a monk from Paris who settled in Lorraine, was a pupil of Gerbert of Aurillac, the scholar who became Pope Sylvester II. He wrote on music in the Pythagorean tradition. The library holds one work under his name, an eleven-page treatise on dividing the monochord in the diatonic genus, printed in PL 151. The work defends Boethius against critics and against Aristoxenus's position: harmonic measure rests on number rather than hearing, consonant ratios are found within twelve or twenty-four, and pipe measures follow monochord number ratios.
b.s: His treatise is a witness to how Gerbert's circle transmitted Boethian music theory to the eleventh century, defending numerical division of the monochord against empiricist accounts of pitch.

w: On the Life of St. Hunegund
On the Translation of the Body of St. Hunegundis at Vermandois

b.bio: A Benedictine monk of Saint-Rémy in Rheims who lived in the tenth century and died in 982. In 948 he led a colony of monks from his convent to Humollières in Vermandois, where he settled the solitary country. The Légendiers latins database styles him abbot there ('ab. Humolariensis'). He wrote two small treatises on St. Hunegund, abbess of Humollières: her Life and an account of the translation of her body at Vermandois, both printed in Migne's PL 137 and inserted by Mabillon in the Acta Ordinis Benedictini.
b.s: His two works here are principal Latin sources for the cult of St. Hunegund, presenting her virginity as a victory over the devil and her baptismal rebirth as the start of sanctity.

b.bio: Berno, a Burgundian monk who entered the Benedictines at St Martin's Abbey, Autun, and later went to Baume, founded Gigny on his own estates about 890 and other houses at Bourg-Dieu (Déols) and Massay. In 909/910 William I, duke of Aquitaine (William the Pious), gave him the territory of Cluny, where he established a monastery dedicated to SS Peter and Paul under the Benedictine rule as reformed by Benedict of Aniane, placed under the immediate authority of the Holy See. Several houses were placed under his care for their reform, notably Déols and Souvigny. He resigned in 925, dividing his abbeys between his relative Vido (Wido) and his disciple Odo, and died on 13 January 927.
b.s: The Testament printed here is the founding charter document of Cluny: it records Berno's division of his monasteries between Wido (who succeeds to Gigny, Baume and Aethicense) and Odo (who succeeds to Cluny, Massay/Macey and Dôle), asserts royal and apostolic privileges protecting the monasteries, and orders that abbots appoint successors while living — provisions that shaped the Cluniac congregation he began.

b.bio: Bernowinus of Clermont (Bernowin) was a ninth-century bishop of Clermont in Auvergne. The old episcopal catalogues leave a gap of about sixty years between Adebert and Stable, and he is thought with some confidence to have filled part of it; French tradition holds that he rebuilt the church of Saint-Alyre in the time of Charlemagne, and his poems show him wealthy and known to the powerful. Verses of his were recovered at Rome in the seventeenth century, including an epitaph for his own tomb. He is not Bernoin, bishop of Besançon around 811.
b.s: The single page held here is a devotional poem on death, sin, and grace: pardon found at the saint's shrine, riches vain before death, the body returning to dust, Christ's cross liberating from the enemy, eternal life given freely by Christ's grace.

w: Life of St. Scholastica the Virgin
On the Fasts Throughout the Year

b.bio: Bertarius (Bertharius) was a Lombard noble who became a monk at Monte Cassino and abbot there in 856, succeeding Bassacius. He fortified the abbey with walls and towers against Muslim raiders between 856 and 873, founded a monastery for women at Teano, and promoted the study of texts. He escaped the Saracen sack of the abbey on September 4, 882 and is venerated as a saint and martyr; sources differ on whether he was killed in 883 or, as McClintock and Strong have it, in 884 while celebrating mass during a siege. The same source's claim that he descended from the French royal family is not confirmed elsewhere.
b.s: The works here are hagiographical and liturgical pieces from PL 126 — a life of St. Scholastica, a treatise on fasts, and verses on St. Benedict — treating prayer, virtue, and monastic discipline.

w: Excerpt in the Deeds of the Bishops of the Church of Verdun

b.bio: Bertarius (Berthaire/Bertharius) of Verdun was a priest and canon at Verdun, also described as a monk of St. Vanne, active between 879 and 925. He wrote the Gesta pontificum sanctae Virdunensis aecclesiae (also edited as Gesta episcoporum Virodunensium), a brief chronicle of the bishops of Verdun to the end of the ninth century, dedicated to Bishop Dadon (880–923). The library holds an Excerpt from this work and a Continuation of it in PL 132.
b.s: His Gesta is a principal source for the early bishops of Verdun, and the works here record episcopal succession, the reform of clerics into monastic communities, and disputes with Count Sigebert, King Lothair, and the monks of Saint Paul.

b.bio: Berthold of Reichenau was a Benedictine monk and chronicler of Reichenau Abbey and a disciple and friend of Hermannus Contractus. When Hermannus saw death approaching, he entrusted Berthold with his wax tablets containing writings not yet committed to parchment, commissioning him to revise and copy them onto parchment, and exhorted him to continue the world-chronicle begun by Hermann, which related the history of the world from the birth of Christ to 1054, the year of Hermann's death. Bernold remarks in his chronicle under the year 1088 that Berthold, an excellent teacher very well versed in Holy Scripture, died at an advanced age on 12 March.
b.s: The works held here are the continuation of Hermann's chronicle and the biography of Hermannus Contractus. As far as written by Berthold, the chronicle is a concise and impartial history of the troublesome times immediately preceding the accession of Pope Gregory VII and probably also of his early reign; the text as printed here treats events including the death of Emperor Henry III in 1056, the minority succession of Henry IV under the empress regent, and the papal succession of Stephen IX after Victor II.

b.bio: The library prints this name as Berthold of Constance; the sources identify him with Bernold of Constance (also Bernaldus, Bernoul), a Swabian priest and chronicler of the Gregorian reform party. Educated at Constance under Bernard of Constance, he attended the Roman Lenten Synod of 1079, was ordained priest on 21 December 1084 by Cardinal Odo (Otto) of Ostia, and entered the Benedictine abbey of St. Blasien, moving in 1091 to All Saints at Schaffhausen, where he died on 16 September 1100. He was an uncompromising opponent of Emperor Henry IV, and continued the chronicle of Hermannus Contractus down to 1100.
b.s: The works held here are his annals of his own times and a eulogy of Peter Damian; his annals are a principal source for the Investiture Contest and the Council of Piacenza, and his tracts defend papal supremacy, excommunication, and the reform decrees of Gregory VII.

b.bio: Bertram of Le Mans (Bertechramnus, Bertichramnus), bishop of Le Mans from 586/587 until his death around 623–626, was one of the wealthiest bishops of sixth-century Gaul. Born near Rouen to a rich landowner, he took the tonsure at Tours and received major orders from Germanus, bishop of Paris, who made him archdeacon. A supporter of Chlotar II, he endured imprisonment under Theudebert II before being restored to his see, attended the Synod of Paris in 614, and left a will disposing of vast estates, endowing churches, freeing his slaves, and providing perpetual alms.
b.s: The work held here is his testament of March 26, 616 — less a theological treatise than a legal-ecclesiastical document whose provisions (the church as sole heir, manumission of slaves, usufruct bequests that do not diminish church property, perpetual alms and lamps for the donor's sins) show how Merovingian piety, property law, and intercessory doctrine were fused in practice.

b.bio: Bertrand de Blanchefort (Blanquefort), born around 1109 in Guyenne as the youngest son of Lord Godfrey de Blanchefort, was the sixth Grand Master of the Knights Templar, holding office from about 1156 or 1157 until his death on 2 January 1169 (13 January by another reckoning). Captured after the defeat at Banyas in 1157, he spent three years imprisoned in Aleppo before release through Byzantine emperor Manuel I Comnenus. He is remembered for reforming the order and favoring negotiation over brute force. The work held here is his letter to King Louis VII of France.
b.s: The library holds his correspondence with Louis VII of France, including a September–October 1163 letter from Bertrand as master of the Temple and the whole Templar convent describing the grave condition of the Latin East—captives and killed magnates, earthquake-damaged fortifications, Baldwin III's death—and begging the king's aid.

w: On the Person and the Two Natures
On the Preaching of the Three Persons
Speculation on the Relationship of Rhetoric
The Art of Geometry and Arithmetic

b.bio: Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, born in Rome into the patrician Anicii family, was orphaned young and raised by Quintus Aurelius Memmius Symmachus, whose daughter Rusticiana he married. He served the Ostrogothic king Theoderic as senator, consul, and magister officiorum before his execution at Pavia around 524–526; the diocese of Pavia honors him as a martyr on 23 October (cult sanctioned 1883). Sources differ slightly on his dates: Wikipedia gives c. 480–524, the Stanford Encyclopedia c. 475–7 to 526?, Routledge c. 480–525/6. His project of translating Greek logic into Latin made him a principal conduit between ancient philosophy and the medieval Latin West.
b.s: The library holds his Latin translations and commentaries on Aristotle's logical corpus (On Interpretation, Categories, Prior and Posterior Analytics, Sophistical Refutations, Topics), Porphyry, Cicero's Topics, the quadrivial works On Music, Arithmetic, and Geometry, and the Consolation of Philosophy — the texts through which Western scholasticism learned its logic.

w: Birth, deeds, and writings of Saint Hildegard
Supplement to the Posthumous Glory of Bruno

b.bio: Bollandiani is the collective name for the Jesuit scholars who edited the Acta Sanctorum, the critical edition of saints' lives begun at Antwerp. The project was conceived by Heribert Rosweyde (d. 1629); Jean Bolland (1596–1665) took it up in 1630, publishing the first volume in 1643, and was joined by Gottfried Henschen and Daniel Papebroch. The works held here under this name are their preliminary commentaries and historical notices prefixed to volumes of Migne's Patrologia Latina — on Hildegard, Bruno of Cologne, Leo IX, John Gualbert, and others — in which they weigh sources, answer objections, and argue points such as Bruno's tenure as master of the schools of Reims and his entry into the Chartreuse in 1084.
b.s: The Bollandists established the critical, source-based method of hagiography, and the commentaries held here are their assessments of the lives and legends of individual saints printed in the Patrologia Latina.

b.bio: Boniface I was bishop of Rome from his disputed election on 28 December 418 until his death on 4 September 422. A Roman priest, son of the presbyter Jocundus according to the Liber Pontificalis, he is believed to have been ordained by Damasus I and to have served as Innocent I's representative at Constantinople around 405. His election against the archdeacon Eulalius produced the fifth Roman schism; Emperor Honorius settled it in Boniface's favor after Eulalius violated an agreement to leave Rome pending a council. He maintained church discipline and restored privileges to the metropolitan sees of Narbonne and Vienne.
b.s: The letters held here concern the legitimacy of his own ordination against Eulalius, appeals of bishops under the Nicene canons (whose authentic text is said to reside with the Greek churches), and the transfer of penitent clerics retaining rank — documents from a contested papal election that shaped rules for episcopal jurisdiction.

b.bio: Boniface II, son of Sigisbald/Sigibuld and of Gothic descent (the first Germanic pope), was archdeacon of the Roman church under Felix IV, who named him successor; he was consecrated 22 September 530 in rivalry with Dioscorus, elected by most Roman priests, whose death weeks later ended the schism. He convoked three Roman synods (530–531), first proposing then annulling a pope's right to designate his successor. The letters held here defend papal authority against certain bishops of Gaul and others, and confirm Caesarius's teaching on grace.
b.s: His letters confirm the Council of Orange's doctrine that grace is always necessary for salvation—prevenient, accompanying, and following the will—and assert the primacy of Peter as the ground of ecclesiastical authority.

b.bio: Boniface IV was born in Valeria to John, a physician of Marsian origin. A deacon of the Roman Church under Gregory I and dispensator of the patrimonies, he was elected pope in 608 after a vacancy of over nine months. With permission from Emperor Phocas he converted the Pantheon into the church of St. Mary and All Martyrs in 609, the first such transformation of a pagan temple at Rome. He encouraged monasticism, presided over a Roman council on monastic discipline in 610, and conferred with Mellitus of London on the needs of the English Church, sending letters to Archbishop Laurence of Canterbury and King Æthelberht.
b.s: The work held here defends monk-priests against those who would exclude monks from priestly office, arguing from Augustine, Gregory, Benedict, Bede, and Boniface that monastic rule bars secular affairs, not priesthood, and that monk-bishops prove monks may bind and loose.

b.bio: Bonifacius V was a Neapolitan who succeeded Deusdedit after a papal vacancy of more than a year and was consecrated on 23 December 619; he died in Rome on 25 October 625. His pontificate fell amid the rebellion of the exarch Eleutherius in war-torn Italy. The Liber Pontificalis credits him with enactments on sanctuary rights and rules for acolytes, and Bede records his letters of encouragement to missionaries in England — to Mellitus of Canterbury and to Justus, first of Rochester and later archbishop of Canterbury. Some letters survive; others are lost.
b.s: The works held here are his letters, chiefly on baptism, church order, and the pallium as metropolitan authority granted by the apostolic see, including one addressed to Justus.

b.bio: Bernard Bottyn was born in Bruges in 1608 and was a Cistercian of Ten Duinen, where he made his profession in 1638; he was ordained subdeacon in 1631, deacon in 1632 and priest on 21 May 1633, and served as prior from 1641. Elected abbot of Ten Duinen in June 1648, his election was confirmed in March 1649 and he received his benediction on 28 March 1649. In 1650 the abbot of Cîteaux, Claude Vaussin, named him vicar general of the Cistercian Order in the Low Countries, with authority to bless abbots and abbesses there. He died on business in Mechelen on 2 October 1653 and was buried in the abbots' crypt at Bruges.
b.s: The library holds under his name a single-page item in PL 210 titled Faculty of the Cistercian Order, consistent with his office as vicar general empowered to confer faculties within the order.

w: On the Finding and Elevation of the Body

b.bio: No surviving record concerns this author — the sources describe Goscelin, Folcuin, and Grimbald of Saint-Bertin, different persons of the same milieu — so nothing is asserted here about his life, dates, or office. The library record shows two Latin works under his name: a Report on the Discovery and Elevation (PL 147) and an account On the Finding and Elevation of the Body (PL 143), evidently concerning the relics of St. Bertin himself, whom he cites. Both are histories of a translation of relics, arguing that saints' elevations should be truthfully recorded in writing (subject to episcopal judgment), that healing is obtained through the merits of the saints, and that the afflictions attending such events come from God's providence rather than chance.
b.s: His works in this collection are written records of the elevation of St. Bertin's relics at Sithiu, defending truthful written commemoration of such translations.

b.bio: No surviving record concerns this author — the sources describe Goscelin, Folcuin, and Grimbald of Saint-Bertin, different persons of the same milieu — so nothing is asserted here about his life, dates, or office. The library record shows two Latin works under his name: a Report on the Discovery and Elevation (PL 147) and an account On the Finding and Elevation of the Body (PL 143), evidently concerning the relics of St. Bertin himself, whom he cites. Both are histories of a translation of relics, arguing that saints' elevations should be truthfully recorded in writing (subject to episcopal judgment), that healing is obtained through the merits of the saints, and that the afflictions attending such events come from God's providence rather than chance.
b.s: His works in this collection are written records of the elevation of St. Bertin's relics at Sithiu, defending truthful written commemoration of such translations.

b.bio: The sources identify Bracilaus only as 'Bracilaus Bohemiae Dux', a duke of Bohemia dated to 1039. Nothing else about his life appears in the records. The library holds one work under his name: the Leges Pro Morum Reformatione, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 151 (cols. 1257–1260A), a short collection of laws for moral reform. The text legislates on marriage as monogamous and indissoluble, prescribes exile rather than slavery for those refusing marital reconciliation, orders clerical denunciation to trigger civil trial and ordeal, bans taverns and Sunday markets and servile work, requires burial in consecrated ground, and exiles capital criminals as Cain-like wanderers — all set against 'the custom of the land'. It cites Adalbert, Severus, and the canons.
b.s: His single held work is an eleventh-century ducal law code on moral reform, showing a lay ruler legislating marriage, worship, and public morals by appeal to canon law against local custom.

b.bio: Bruno of Segni was born at Solero in Piedmont around 1048 and educated at Bologna before becoming a canon of Siena. Called to Rome for his learning, he served as counsellor to four popes, compelled Berengar of Tours to retract his denial of the real presence at the synod of 1079, and was consecrated Bishop of Segni by Gregory VII in 1080. He accompanied Urban II to Clermont in 1095, entered Monte Cassino as a monk in 1102, and later returned to his see. He denounced lay investiture as heretical. He must not be confused with Bruno of Cologne, founder of the Carthusians (d. 1101), or with Bruno the Saxon chronicler.
b.s: The library holds his Gregoriale (PL 155), an exposition of Job built on Gregory the Great, characteristic of his scriptural writing in the reform-era church.

b.bio: None of The surviving records identifies this Bruno. They describe three different men: Bruno the Saxon, an eleventh-century chronicler of the Saxon war against Henry IV; St. Bruno of Cologne (c. 1030–1101), founder of the Carthusians; and Ulrich of Strasbourg, a thirteenth-century Dominican. None matches the library's single item under this name: a letter addressed to Gerhoh of Reichersberg printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 166, where Gerhoh's own correspondence is collected. The letter belongs to the circle of twelfth-century reform writers around Gerhoh, but the sources give no dates, office, or biography for its author.
b.s: The library holds one short letter to Gerhoh of Reichersberg (PL 166), evidence of correspondence within Gerhoh's Gregorian reform network rather than a substantial body of doctrine.

w: Letter to the clergy of Langres

b.bio: Bruno of Langres was bishop of Langres until his death on 30 January 1016. He was a son of Ragenold de Roucy and Alberade of Reims (per genealogical record), belonged to the Burgundian nobility aligned with the Carolingians rather than the rising Capetian dynasty, and his successor Lambert I was elected under King Robert II's influence. He directed the renovation of the abbatial basilica of Saint-Bénigne de Dijon. The works held here — a letter to his clergy, a charter, and a letter to Heldric — treat confession, repentance, and conversion: sins must be confessed to obtain forgiveness, true repentance is amendment rather than repetition of sin, God wills the conversion of the sinner not his death, and no quantity of sins exceeds God's mercy.
b.s: His surviving letters show a tenth-century bishop preaching penitential reform to his own clergy, grounding confession in Ezekiel, the Gospels, and James.

b.bio: A Saxon cleric of the second half of the eleventh century, attached to the household of Archbishop Werner of Magdeburg, a leader of the Saxon uprising against Henry IV. After Werner's death in 1078 Bruno attached himself to Werner, Bishop of Merseburg, to whom he dedicated his Historia de Bello Saxonico in 1082. The work narrates Henry IV's youth and misrule, the causes and course of the Saxon rebellions, and ends with the election of Hermann of Luxemburg as king in 1081.
b.s: His History of the Saxon War is the principal contemporary Saxon account of the revolt against Henry IV, justifying the rebellion and the election of Rudolf as anti-king while preserving ten letters of Gregory VII and the 'Saxon letters' exchanged with the rebels — key evidence for the Regnum–Sacerdotium conflict.

w: Notice concerning the restoration of the monastery of Saint Aper

b.bio: Bruno of Toul is the name under which the library holds the pre-papal writings of Bruno, count of Egisheim and Dagsburg, born at Egisheim in Alsace on 21 June 1002 and educated in the household of Berthold, bishop of Toul. He became bishop of Toul and was elected pope in 1049, taking the name Leo IX; he died in Rome on 19 April 1054. The two items held here are not treatises but episcopal documents: diplomas and a notice concerning the restoration of the monastery of Saint-Aper, recording grants, vicars appointed by patrons, the reservation of altar dues to the bishop, and the conditions under which donations to monks revert.
b.s: The works here show Leo IX's own practice as bishop of Toul — property, patronage, and monastic restoration — rather than his better-known papal reform legislation.

b.bio: Burgundofara, also called Fara, was born around 595 to a noble family near Meaux. Consecrated as a child by Columbanus, she resisted her father Agneric's attempt to marry her off, with Eustathius intervening on her side, and founded the double monastery of Faremoutiers in the Brie, which she led for some forty years. The date of her death is uncertain: sources give 643 or 655 in one place and a range of 641 to 664 in another. The work held here is not a theological treatise but her will, dated 26 October in the fifth regnal year of Dagobert I (633/634), recording donations of villas, serfs, and toll-rights to the monastery built in honour of Mary and Peter.
b.s: Her testament is one of the earliest surviving documents showing how a Merovingian noblewoman endowed a monastery, pairing pious donation with legal sanctions against infringers drawn from Theodosian law.

b.bio: Benedetto Chelonio is Benedict Chelidonius (Schwalbe), a monk from the Nuremberg area who became abbot of the Scottish monastery in Vienna in 1518 and died there on 8 September 1521. A Neo-Latin poet, he wrote verses for Albrecht Dürer's woodcut cycles of 1511 and was a friend of Johann Eck. In 1519 he published an edition of Bandinus's twelfth-century Sentences, an abridgement of Peter Lombard which Chelidonius mistakenly took for Lombard's model.
b.s: The two short pieces held here are his prefatory letters to that Bandinus edition, where he surveys citations and argues that Bandinus's summary parallels the Lombard's Sentences.

b.bio: Born Charles d'Affringues at Saint-Omer on 20 April 1549, he studied philosophy, theology, medicine, and ancient languages at Paris, took a doctorate in civil and canon law, and served as canon of Carpentras, vicar general, and official of the vice-legate at Avignon before entering La Grande Chartreuse in 1590, taking the religious name Bruno. Professed on 1 April 1591, he became prior of the Charterhouse of Avignon (1594), visitor for Provence (1599), and was elected prior of La Grande Chartreuse and general minister of the order on 4 February 1600, serving until 1630. He corresponded with Francis de Sales and edited the folio Carthusian Missal (Paris, Jamet Mettayer, 1603).
b.s: The single item held here, a testament printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 152, is attributed to him by the library record, though that volume otherwise collects texts from centuries earlier and the attribution warrants caution.

w: Act of the Election of Gerbert
Acts of the Election of Arnulf

b.bio: This entry covers two short election acts preserved under the name of the bishops of Reims in Migne's PL 139: the Act of the Election of Gerbert and the Acts of the Election of Arnulf. The texts cite Hugh Capet, King Robert, Adalbero, and Remigius as authorities.
b.s: These acts are primary evidence for how a medieval metropolitan church argued episcopal legitimacy: consent of clergy and people, freedom from simony, personal virtue and learning as qualifications, no see vacant beyond thirty days, purification of the tainted for office, division of sees preserving unity rather than schism, and confirmation by subscription of the faithful.

w: Charter for the monastery of Saint Michael

b.bio: The library prints this author only as 'Bishop of Avranches,' and the work it holds under the name is a charter for the monastery of Saint Michael, printed in PL 147. The charter's content matches what is known of John of Avranches, a Norman churchman, son of Rodulf of Ivry and brother of Hugh of Bayeux, who held the see of Avranches from 1060 to 1067 before becoming archbishop of Rouen when Lanfranc declined that post. As archbishop he pursued reform, campaigning for clerical celibacy from 1074 — a campaign that got him stoned at a provincial synod — and in 1075 he and Roger de Beaumont effectively governed Normandy. He should not be confused with Achard of Saint-Victor, a later bishop of the same see (died 1171), whose works were De trinitate and sermons.
b.s: The charter here shows an eleventh-century Norman bishop allocating jurisdiction: the abbot exercises delegated archidiaconal authority, marriage dissolution rests on witnessed testimony, ordination, degradation, ordeal judgments, chrism, and excommunication all remain anchored to the episcopal see.

b.bio: None of The surviving records identifies this author. They describe several unrelated men named Gualterus or Bernardus Walterus: Walter of Bruges, a thirteenth-century Franciscan bishop of Poitiers; Gualterus Anglicus, a twelfth-century fabulist; Bernhard Walther Marperger, a Lutheran pastor; and Walter of Saint-Victor, prior of Saint-Victor in Paris, dead by 1180. None matches the library's holdings, which are two short dedicatory letters on the Carthusians' perpetual spiritual warfare against Satan, one invoking Bruno. The attribution to any named figure is unsupported, so no dates, offices, or biography are asserted here.
b.s: The works held under this name are two brief dedicatory letters presenting the Carthusian order as engaged in unceasing combat with Satan, with appeal to Bruno as the order's founder.

b.bio: No biographical information is available for this author. The supplied web sources all concern Benjamin Hoffmann, a contemporary French novelist and professor at Ohio State University (b. 1985), who is plainly not the author of this Latin treatise on the paschal cycle in PL 67; per policy, those sources cannot be used for this note, so no biographical facts are asserted here.
b.s: The single work held is a 16-page historical argument that Dionysius restored rather than invented the nineteen-year paschal cycle, tracing it to Meton's Greek astronomy and crediting Anatolius with its first application to Easter, against Joannes Noviomagus, Dionysius Exiguus as commonly read, and those who attribute the enneadecaeteris to Nicaea.

b.bio: Humbert of Moyenmoutier entered the Benedictine abbey of Moyenmoutier in Lorraine around 1015 and studied law and theology there. Pope Leo IX brought him to Rome late in 1049, made him archbishop of Sicily, then cardinal bishop of Silva Candida in 1050. He condemned Berengarius of Tours in 1050, served as legate at Benevento in 1051, and in 1054 was legate to Constantinople, where he excommunicated Patriarch Michael Cerularius. He died in Rome on 5 May 1061.
b.s: The single-page epistle held here argues that faithful teachers supply what the church needs, that vigilant teachers are formed by Scripture read with patristic authority, and that brief open exposition is better than prolix obscure speech.

w: Inquiry into the Epoch of the Catalogue

b.bio: Corporate authorship by the Benedictine community restored at Solesmes in 1833 by Prosper Guéranger (1805–1875), who re-established Benedictine monastic life in France after it had been wiped out by the French Revolution and rebuilt the monastery as a center of scholarship. The two pieces held here are editorial apparatus printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina, volume 13: a preface and an inquiry into the date of the Liberian Catalogue of popes. In them the monks argue that Damasus compiled the catalogue in 354, that its unfinished consular date proves composition under Liberius, that Felix IV's catalogue depends on it, and that Roman Christians dated bishops by consular fasti. They defend these claims against Dodwell, Pearson, Dom Ceillier, Papebrock, and Schelstrate.
b.s: Their defense of the Liberian Catalogue's authenticity and consular dating remains part of the critical apparatus surrounding one of the oldest documents of the Roman episcopal list.

w: Inquiry into the Life and Writings of Othloh
On the Life and Writings of Gerhoh

b.bio: Bernhard Pez, born at Ybbs near Melk on 22 February 1683 and died at Melk on 27 March 1735, was an Austrian Benedictine historian and librarian. He entered Melk Abbey in 1699, studied theology at the University of Vienna, was ordained priest in 1708, and became librarian at Melk in 1713. Following the model of the French Maurists, he searched monastic archives and libraries in Austria, Bavaria, and Swabia with his brother Hieronymus Pez, and in 1716 published a plan for a universal Benedictine library cataloguing all authors of the order; he gathered over seven hundred titles for it.
b.s: The works held here are his editorial apparatus — notices, admonitions, and studies of Gerhoh of Reichersberg and Othloh — by which he introduced medieval Benedictine writers to readers of the Patrologia Latina volumes.

b.bio:
Pez, Bernhard (1683–1735) — Bernhard Pez, born at Ybbs near Melk, entered Melk Abbey in 1699, studied theology at Vienna, was ordained priest in 1708, and became librarian at Melk in 1713. With his brother Hieronymus he searched Austrian, Bavarian, and Swabian monasteries for manuscripts (1715–17), following the French Maurists as a model. In 1716 he proposed a universal Benedictine library cataloguing all authors of the order, gathering over seven hundred titles.

Pez, Hieronymus (c. 1685–1762) — Hieronymus Pez was born at Ybbs on 24 February 1685 and entered the novitiate at Melk Abbey in 1703, where he was ordained in 1711. He assisted his brother Bernhard in searching Austrian, Bavarian, and Swabian monastic archives for manuscripts from 1714 onward, and after Bernhard's death became librarian at Melk, remaining there until his death on 14 October 1762. His chief work is the Scriptores rerum Austriacarum (1721–1745), a three-volume collection of over a hundred sources for Austrian history, many of which have never been re-edited. He also published Acta S. Colomanni (1713) and a history of St. Leopold (1746/47), and belonged to the Societas eruditorum incognitorum in terris Austriacis.
b.s: He matters less as an author than as an editor: the two short Latin pieces held here — an admonition (PL 131) and a notice on Theodoric (PL 147) — are editorial items from his manuscript collections rather than compositions of his own.

b.bio:
Beatus Rhenanus (1485–1547) — Beatus Rhenanus, born Beatus Bild at Schlettstadt (Sélestat) in Alsace, studied at Paris under Lefèvre d'Étaples and took the master of arts degree there. From 1511 he worked in Basel as one of the scholars editing texts for Johann Froben, where he became a close collaborator of Erasmus. His editions include the first printed edition of Tertullian (1521), Curtius Rufus, and Velleius Paterculus, and he was ennobled by the Emperor. He died at Strasbourg.

Andreas Hoy (unknown) — No source identifies this author. The name as printed here ('Andreas Hoy') must not be confused with Andreas Hoyer (1661–1725), the Lutheran Generalsuperintendent recorded in Deutsche Biographie, whose career and confession do not fit a Latin patristic treatise held in PL 1; the match in name alone does not establish identity. What can be said comes from the work itself: 'Proverbial Formulae' is a citation-survey and exegetical study that leans overwhelmingly on Tertullian (60 citations), with Cicero, Virgil, Pliny, Horace and Homer also cited, and it names the editors Rhenanus and Pamelius among its authorities, placing its composition in the circle of early modern Tertullian scholarship.
b.s: The work held here shows him as a philologist rather than a systematic theologian: a citation-survey of proverbial formulae, built chiefly from Tertullian, arguing that pagan proverbs preserve truths such as the soul's departure from the body and the resurrection, and that Marcion's excisions leave great gaps in Scripture.

w: On the Author of the Following Works

b.bio: Bertrand Tissier (Latinized Textor), born at Rumigny in the Ardennes around 1600 and died at Blanchefosse-et-Bay in 1672, was a monk of Bonnefontaine Abbey, attested there by 12 March 1622. He studied at the Jesuit university of Pont-à-Mousson, took a doctorate in theology, served as prior of Bonnefontaine in 1641, and introduced the Strict Observance to his house in 1664. He is chiefly remembered for the eight-volume Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium, printed at the abbey's own press, collecting writings of Cistercian fathers of Bernard's age; he also wrote defenses of church teaching against Protestantism and Jansenism. The notices held here are his prefatory biographies of authors whose works that collection edited.
b.s: His Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium preserved and made accessible the principal texts of the first generations of Cistercian writers; the pieces here are his editorial notices on figures such as Isaac of Stella, Guerric, and Aelred.

b.bio: Bernardo Maria de Rubeis (born Giovanni Francesco de Rossi) was born at Cividale del Friuli on 8 January 1687 to a noble family. He took the Dominican habit at Conegliano in 1703, studied at S. Marco in Florence and at the convent of the Rosario alle Zattere in Venice, where he taught theology until he gave up the chair (sources differ: 1750 or 1730). He traveled to Vienna in 1718, compiling a catalogue of Dominican writers' works in the imperial library, and accompanied a Venetian embassy to Paris, where he met Echard, Lequien, and Montfaucon. He edited Aquinas with commentary (1745–60, 24 vols.) and wrote De Peccato Originali (1757).
b.s: The two pieces held here are his historical clarifications on Chromatius of Aquileia, arguing that the Roman bishop Chromatius is the Aquileian bishop consecrated/ordained by Ambrose as Valerian's successor in 388, that he was Spanish by birth, that he instigated Jerome's Latin translation from Hebrew, and that Origen's books must be forbidden to the faithful — against Rufinus, Jerome, Justus Fontaninus, Theophilus of Alexandria, and Pagi.
